chapter_title: GameObjects and Components: The Core of Unity
chapter_summary:
At the heart of every Unity project, whether it's a complex VR simulation or a simple AR experience, are **GameObjects**. A GameObject is the most fundamental entity in Unity – it's essentially an empty container that doesn't do anything on its own. Think of a GameObject as a blank canvas or an empty box. It doesn't have a shape, a color, or any behavior until you add something to it. Every item you see in your scene, from a virtual tree to a player character, a camera, or even an invisible manager for game logic, is a GameObject. When you create a new 3D object like a Cube or a Sphere, Unity actually creates a GameObject and automatically attaches several default components to it to give it its initial appearance and properties. You can also create an empty GameObject by right-clicking in the Hierarchy and selecting `Create Empty`. These are incredibly useful for organizing your scene, acting as parent containers for other objects, or holding scripts that manage global game logic.

The real power and functionality of GameObjects come from **Components**. If a GameObject is an empty box, then Components are the specialized tools, features, and behaviors you put inside that box. Every single piece of functionality a GameObject possesses is provided by a Component attached to it. For example, to make a GameObject visible, you need a `Mesh Filter` (to define its shape) and a `Mesh Renderer` (to draw that shape with a material). To make it respond to physics, you need a `Rigidbody` and a `Collider`. To make it interactive, you attach a custom C# script, which itself is a Component. This component-based architecture is a cornerstone of Unity's flexibility and power. It allows you to mix and match functionalities, creating highly customized objects without having to rewrite entire classes from scratch.

Let's explore some of the most common and essential Components you'll encounter. The `Transform` component is unique and always present on every GameObject; you cannot remove it. It defines the GameObject's position, rotation, and scale in 3D space. We briefly touched on this in the previous chapter, but it's worth reiterating its importance. The values in the Transform component are what you manipulate with the Move, Rotate, and Scale tools. For AR/VR, precise control over these values is paramount for aligning virtual objects with the real world or for creating believable virtual environments. Another pair of crucial components for visual objects are the `Mesh Filter` and `Mesh Renderer`. The `Mesh Filter` holds the 3D model's mesh data (the actual shape of the object), while the `Mesh Renderer` takes that mesh and draws it in the scene using a specified material. Without both, your object won't be visible.

For physics interactions, `Colliders` are indispensable. A Collider component defines the physical shape of a GameObject for collision detection. It doesn't make the object visible, but it defines its boundaries for interactions. Common types include `Box Collider`, `Sphere Collider`, `Capsule Collider`, and `Mesh Collider`. Without a collider, objects will simply pass through each other. To make an object respond to physics forces (like gravity, impacts, or pushes), you also need to attach a `Rigidbody` component. The Rigidbody gives the GameObject mass, drag, and allows it to be affected by physics. A common mistake is forgetting to add a Collider or Rigidbody to an object that needs to interact physically, leading to objects falling through the floor or not reacting to collisions. Always ensure your interactive objects have appropriate colliders and rigidbodies.

Adding and removing components is straightforward via the Inspector window. When you select a GameObject, the Inspector displays all its attached components. You can click the `Add Component` button at the bottom of the Inspector and search for the component you need. To remove a component, click the small gear icon next to its name in the Inspector and select `Remove Component`. Configuring component properties is done directly in the Inspector, where you'll find various fields, checkboxes, and sliders for each component. For instance, a `Box Collider` has properties for its size and center, while a `Rigidbody` has properties for mass, gravity, and constraints. Understanding how to effectively use and configure these components is fundamental to building any interactive experience in Unity, especially for AR/VR where precise physical interactions and visual representations are key to immersion.

screens.title: GameObjects and Components
screens.subtitle: The building blocks that give every Unity scene its shape, behavior, and physics.

narration.text: In Unity, nearly everything you place into a scene starts life as a GameObject — an intentionally empty container that becomes meaningful only when you attach Components to it. Think of a GameObject as a chassis or a blank box: it holds parts but does nothing by itself. Components are those parts: a Transform that places the object in space, a Mesh Filter and Mesh Renderer that make it visible, a Collider and Rigidbody that let it interact physically, and scripts that define custom behavior. In practical AR and VR work this pattern matters because you can combine and swap Components to iterate quickly without rewriting core classes. For example, a single GameObject can be reused as a visual prop with a Mesh Renderer, then reused again as a physics object by adding a Rigidbody. A common misunderstanding is to expect a newly created GameObject to behave like a fully formed object — it will not, until Components are attached. As you explore this chapter, notice how Components compose functionality and how the Inspector becomes your primary tool for adding, configuring, and removing those Components. By the end you will be able to assemble visible, interactive, and physics-enabled objects from simple building blocks — and you will understand why Unity chose this modular design.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: GameObjects are empty containers; Components provide all functionality. Combine components to compose visible, interactive, and physical objects.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › GameObjects and Components
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

GameObjects & Components

Understand how empty GameObjects become visible, physical, and interactive through attached Components. This composition model is the basis of all Unity scenes, from simple AR overlays to complex VR simulations.

In this lesson
What a GameObject is and how Components add behavior.
Coming up
Common Components: Transform, Mesh, Collider, Rigidbody.
Hands-on
Build a simple physics scene to see components in action.
Why this matters

Component composition lets you reuse, iterate, and combine capabilities. In AR/VR, that speed and flexibility translates directly into prototyping interactive experiences and aligning virtual content with the real world.

Visual Concept
Composable parts make the object
GameObject (empty)
A blank container that holds Components. No visual or physical behavior by itself.
Components
Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, Collider, Rigidbody, and scripts attach to add capability.
Combine components to convert the empty container into a visible, interactive, or physical object.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will define and work confidently with GameObjects and Components in Unity. You will be able to explain what a GameObject is and why it acts as an empty container in the scene, and you will name the Transform as the mandatory component every GameObject carries. You will also understand how Components such as Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, Collider, and Rigidbody each provide a distinct role — one for shape, one for drawing, and others for physical boundaries and physics response. Practically, you will add, remove, and configure Components using the Inspector, including adjusting collider sizes and Rigidbody mass. Finally you will reason about parent–child relationships so you can organize scenes and rely on hierarchical transforms for grouped movement. Each objective maps to a hands-on skill: creating a visible object, enabling its collisions, tuning physics, and nesting objects for coordinated transformations. Keep an eye out for a common pitfall: assuming a primitive is fully functional without the correct collider or Rigidbody for the intended interaction. That misconception is easy to catch once you test your scene in Play mode.

keyIdea.title: Learning focus
keyIdea.text: Define GameObjects, attach Components, configure Transform/physics, and use parent-child hierarchies to structure scenes.

screens.title: What is a GameObject?
screens.subtitle: An empty container that becomes useful only after you attach Components.

narration.text: A GameObject in Unity is best understood as an empty container — a blank box or chassis — that holds Components to define its behavior and appearance. It does not intrinsically have shape, color, or physics. This means when you add a Cube primitive, Unity creates a GameObject and then attaches default Components like a Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, and usually a Collider. The key practical point is that the identity of an object in a scene is the GameObject, while the capabilities come from its Components. For example, to make an object visible you need both a Mesh Filter and a Mesh Renderer: the Mesh Filter holds the mesh geometry while the Mesh Renderer draws it with a material. A common misconception is to treat primitives or visual assets as self-contained objects; in Unity, these are still GameObjects with attached Components. Because GameObjects are just containers, you can create an empty GameObject to act as a scene organizer or a parent for multiple children; it can hold manager scripts without any visible shape. In AR/VR workflows this composability is helpful: you can attach tracking scripts or alignment helpers to empty GameObjects and reuse them across scenes. Reflect on this: if an object behaves wrongly, check the GameObject's attached Components first — that is where behavior lives.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: GameObject = empty container. Function comes from attached Components, not from the container itself.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is a GameObject?
Definition & Metaphor

A GameObject is an empty container. Imagine a car chassis that needs an engine, wheels, and seats — the chassis itself doesn’t drive until parts are attached. Similarly, a GameObject becomes useful only when Components are attached.

Example
Create an empty GameObject and attach a script later to manage global logic. It remains invisible until you add rendering components.
Misconception
Assuming a primitive is fully functional just because it looks like an object. Visibility and physics are separate components.
Key Takeaway

Treat the GameObject as the holder; check components to understand behavior.

Visual breakdown
GameObject
Empty container; holds Components like Transform and custom scripts.
Components
Attach to give shape, physics, and behavior: Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, Collider, Rigidbody, etc.
Concrete scenario
You make a Cube primitive. Unity gives it a Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, and a Box Collider. If the Cube should fall, you add a Rigidbody. Check components to diagnose why it isn’t colliding or moving.

screens.title: Components: How functionality is added
screens.subtitle: Components provide visuals, physics, and behavior to GameObjects.

narration.text: Components are modular pieces you attach to a GameObject to give it specific properties or behaviors. Each Component handles one concern: the Transform handles position, rotation, and scale; the Mesh Filter holds mesh geometry; the Mesh Renderer draws that mesh with a material; Colliders define boundaries for collisions; Rigidbody enables physics response. Think of Components like tools you add to a toolbox — when combined they produce an object that is visible, collidable, and interactive. A concrete example: to make a ball that bounces, the GameObject needs a Mesh Filter with a sphere mesh, a Mesh Renderer to render it, a Sphere Collider to define its collision shape, and a Rigidbody to respond to gravity and impulses. A frequent mistake is adding only a Renderer and expecting collision behavior; without a Collider and Rigidbody the object will not participate in physics. Another common area of confusion is the Transform: because it is required and always present, learners sometimes try to remove it; Unity prevents this because every object must have a position in space. As you attach Components, configure their properties in the Inspector — for example, set Rigidbody mass or collider size — and test changes in Play mode to see the live effect. When you think about design, favor small, focused Components rather than monolithic scripts; composition improves reusability and clarity.

keyIdea.title: Component principle
keyIdea.text: Each Component addresses a single role. Combine them to compose complex behavior without rewriting core systems.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Components
What each Component does
Transform
Always present. Defines position, rotation, and scale in 3D space.
Mesh Filter + Mesh Renderer
Mesh Filter stores geometry; Mesh Renderer renders it with a material so the object is visible.
Collider + Rigidbody
Collider defines collision boundaries; Rigidbody makes the GameObject respond to physics forces.
Concrete example
To make a bouncing ball: attach a Sphere Mesh Filter, Sphere Mesh Renderer, Sphere Collider, and a Rigidbody. Create a Physics Material with high bounciness and assign it to the collider. Play the scene to confirm the ball bounces instead of passing through the floor.
Common mistake
Expecting Mesh Renderer alone to enable collisions. A visible mesh without a collider will not interact physically.
Key Takeaway

Attach focused Components and test in Play mode to verify their combined effect.

screens.title: Transform: Position, Rotation, Scale
screens.subtitle: The mandatory component that anchors every GameObject in space.

narration.text: The Transform component is unique: every GameObject has one and it cannot be removed. Transform stores three fundamental properties: position, rotation, and scale. Position places the object in world or local coordinates, rotation orients it, and scale stretches or shrinks it. In AR/VR contexts precise Transform values are essential for aligning virtual content with the real world and for maintaining believable interactions. For example, placing a virtual cup on a real table requires matching position and rotation closely so the cup looks anchored. A common pitfall is confusing local and global coordinates: a child's position is relative to its parent, so moving the parent moves the child, but the child's local values remain unchanged. Practically, use the Move, Rotate, and Scale editor tools and watch the Transform fields update in the Inspector. When you animate or script motion, you modify Transform values either directly or through physics (Rigidbody should be used for physics-driven movement). Remember: changing scale can affect collider sizes and visual fidelity. A final quick check: if a spawned object appears off-screen, inspect its Transform first — incorrect position or parented transform is the most likely culprit.

keyIdea.title: Transform essentials
keyIdea.text: Transform defines where and how an object sits in space. Understand local vs global coordinates and test changes visually.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Transform
Transform fields
  • Position: X, Y, Z coordinates in either local or world space.
  • Rotation: orient the object; watch for gimbal rotation in Euler angles.
  • Scale: change the size; non-uniform scaling can distort meshes and colliders.
Example: Parent a virtual lamp to an empty GameObject that tracks a table. When the table moves, the lamp follows because its position is relative to the parent's Transform.
Misconception: Setting a child's global position is the same as changing its local position. They differ: global updates its world coordinates, local updates its coordinates relative to parent.
Practical tips
Use local coordinates for grouped animations and world coordinates for absolute placement.
When precision is required in AR, enter Transform values numerically to match real-world measurements.
If physics drives motion, prefer Rigidbody-based movement over manual Transform changes to avoid conflicts.
Key Takeaway

Master local vs world transforms and prefer Rigidbody for physics-driven motion to avoid transform conflicts.

screens.title: Mesh Filter and Mesh Renderer
screens.subtitle: How geometry and materials make objects visible in the scene.

narration.text: Visual objects require two cooperating Components: a Mesh Filter and a Mesh Renderer. The Mesh Filter holds the mesh data: the vertices, edges, and faces that define shape. The Mesh Renderer takes that mesh and draws it to the screen using a material that defines color, texture, and surface properties. Without a Mesh Filter there is no geometry to draw; without a Mesh Renderer there is nothing that tells Unity to render the mesh. For example, when you create a Cube primitive, Unity adds a Mesh Filter with cube geometry and a Mesh Renderer with a default material so you immediately see the cube. In AR/VR work you will often swap meshes or change materials at runtime to reflect different states, like changing a material to indicate selection. A misstep is to expect visual changes to affect physics automatically — changing a Mesh Renderer or material does not update colliders; if you alter mesh geometry at runtime, ensure colliders still match the visible shape or update the collider appropriately. When troubleshooting a missing object, verify both Mesh Filter and Mesh Renderer are present and that the material isn’t set to invisible or the mesh isn’t empty.

keyIdea.title: Visual pipeline
keyIdea.text: Mesh Filter provides geometry; Mesh Renderer uses materials to draw that geometry. Both are required for visibility.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Mesh Filter & Renderer
Roles explained
Mesh Filter: stores mesh geometry (vertices, triangles).
Mesh Renderer: renders that mesh using a material and lighting.
Example: Cube primitive includes both so the object is visible immediately.
Practical notes
If you change the mesh at runtime, ensure colliders still match the visible shape. Materials affect appearance but not physics. Use materials to indicate states like selection or damage without changing physical properties.
Check this when invisible
Verify Mesh Filter has a valid mesh and Mesh Renderer is enabled with a readable material. An empty Mesh Filter results in no visible geometry.
Key Takeaway

Visibility requires both mesh data and a renderer. Changes to appearance don’t imply physics changes.

screens.title: Colliders: Defining physical boundaries
screens.subtitle: How colliders allow collision detection without affecting visibility.

narration.text: Colliders define the physical boundaries of GameObjects for collision detection. They do not render anything by themselves; instead, they give the physics engine a shape to test for overlaps and contacts. Common types include Box Collider, Sphere Collider, Capsule Collider, and Mesh Collider. For most primitives a primitive collider such as a Box or Sphere provides efficient collision checks. A Mesh Collider uses mesh geometry to closely match complex shapes but is more costly. For example, if you want a character to walk around a table, add a Box Collider to the table representation so the character's collider detects the surface and sides. A frequent error is forgetting to add any collider; in that case, objects will pass through each other despite being visible. Another nuance is Is Trigger: when set, the collider reports overlap events but does not perform a physical response, which is useful for triggers and pickups. When pairing colliders with physics responses, ensure that at least one of the colliding objects has a Rigidbody; otherwise Unity treats collisions as static interactions and certain callbacks behave differently. Always profile complex scenes where many mesh colliders might hurt performance.

keyIdea.title: Collider role
keyIdea.text: Colliders tell Unity where objects can touch or overlap; they are required for collisions but separate from rendering.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Colliders
Collider types
  • Box Collider — efficient for cuboid shapes.
  • Sphere Collider — efficient for round shapes.
  • Capsule Collider — useful for characters.
  • Mesh Collider — matches complex geometry, more expensive.
Use Is Trigger when you need overlap events but no physical collision response, such as pickups or zone detection.
Practical scenario
To keep a player from walking through a virtual table, ensure the table has a Collider that matches its shape and the player has an appropriate Collider and, typically, a Rigidbody. If the table is static, it can omit a Rigidbody; the player will still collide with the static collider.
Common mistake: expecting visual fidelity from a collider. Mesh Colliders provide shape accuracy, but they can harm performance. Use primitives where possible and combine colliders for complex objects.
Key Takeaway

Colliders define interaction boundaries. Match collider type to shape and performance needs.

screens.title: Rigidbody: Enabling physics
screens.subtitle: Make objects respond to gravity, forces, and collisions.

narration.text: The Rigidbody component enables a GameObject to participate in Unity's physics system. Adding a Rigidbody gives mass, drag, and enables responses to gravity and external forces. With a Rigidbody, collisions detected by Colliders become physically simulated: objects can fall, bounce, and push each other. For instance, adding a Rigidbody to a Cube placed above a Plane makes the Cube fall under gravity and stop when its collider contacts the Plane. You can tune Rigidbody properties such as Mass to change how heavy it feels, and Drag to simulate air resistance. One common mistake is to mix manual Transform changes with physics-driven motion: if you move a Rigidbody-controlled object by directly setting Transform values each frame, you can create non-physical behaviour and conflicts. Instead, when using Rigidbody, prefer applying forces or using Rigidbody's movement methods for consistent simulation. Another important note is that static colliders and dynamic rigidbodies interact differently: static colliders without a Rigidbody remain immovable, which is efficient for floors and walls. As you experiment, try increasing mass dramatically or making a collider a trigger to observe the different outcomes. Ask yourself how mass and collider choice will affect the user’s sense of realism in AR/VR.

keyIdea.title: Physics activation
keyIdea.text: Adding a Rigidbody gives an object mass and lets physics govern motion. Use Rigidbody methods rather than direct Transform changes for physics-driven objects.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Rigidbody
Rigidbody properties
Mass — how heavy the object behaves.
Drag — simulates air resistance.
Use Gravity checkbox and constraints to control motion axes.
Example test
Place Cube at Y=5, Plane at Y=0, add Rigidbody to Cube. Play the scene and observe the Cube fall and rest on the Plane. Modify Mass to feel the difference when hitting another object.
Misuse: Changing Transform.position every frame for a Rigidbody object can cause non-physical behavior. Use forces or Rigidbody.MovePosition for physics-driven motion.
Key Takeaway

Use Rigidbody to let physics govern movement and collisions; tune properties for realistic responses.

screens.title: Add, Configure, and Remove Components
screens.subtitle: Using the Inspector to shape object behavior step by step.

narration.text: The Inspector is Unity’s primary interface for working with Components on a selected GameObject. The typical workflow is straightforward and repeatable. First, select a GameObject in the Hierarchy so the Inspector shows its current Components. Second, click Add Component and search for the Component you need — for instance, Rigidbody — and add it. Third, configure the Component’s fields: set Rigidbody mass, toggle gravity, or adjust the Box Collider size and center. Fourth, test the scene in Play mode to see the live effect; if behavior is not as expected, return to the Inspector to tweak values. To remove a Component, use the gear icon on the Component and select Remove Component. A practical example: to make a Cube fall and bounce, add a Rigidbody, verify the Cube already has a Box Collider, create a Physics Material with high bounciness, and assign it to the collider’s Material slot. A common beginner mistake is modifying values only during Play mode and then forgetting to apply them; remember that changes during Play are not saved. When collaborating, annotate GameObjects with clear names and, when necessary, use empty GameObjects as parents to keep configurations tidy.

keyIdea.title: Inspector workflow
keyIdea.text: Select → Add Component → Configure fields → Test in Play → Remove if unwanted. Avoid changing values only during Play mode unless intentional.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Add / Configure / Remove
Step-by-step
1
Select the GameObject and inspect current Components.
2
Click Add Component, search the Component name, and add it to the GameObject.
3
Adjust properties in the Inspector (e.g., mass, collider size) and test in Play mode.
4
To remove, open the Component gear and choose Remove Component.
Example: Add Rigidbody
Select Cube → Add Component → Rigidbody → set Mass to 1 → Play to observe gravity. If Cube lacks a collider, add Box Collider first.
Remember: changes made only during Play are not saved. Make required adjustments outside Play or reapply them after testing.
Key Takeaway

The Inspector is your control panel: add, tune, and remove Components, then verify behavior in Play mode.

screens.title: Parent-Child Relationships
screens.subtitle: How hierarchical transforms create grouped movement and local transforms.

narration.text: Parent-child relationships let you organize and coordinate GameObjects so children inherit the parent's Transform. When you parent objects, a child's position, rotation, and scale become relative to its parent. This is powerful for grouping complex models or creating moving assemblies: move or rotate the parent to affect every child simultaneously. For example, in AR you might parent a virtual lamp and its shade to an empty GameObject that tracks a real table; moving the table will move both the lamp and shade together. A common confusion arises around local versus global transforms. Local values are shown in the Inspector when an object is a child; the world position is computed from the parent's transforms. If you need a child to keep a global position when reparenting, capture its world coordinates, reparent, and then set its local transform accordingly. Hierarchies are also essential for animation rigs and for organizing scene structure: using empty GameObjects as parents is a lightweight way to control groups. Watch out for unexpected scaling: a parent with non-uniform scale affects children and can distort colliders and meshes. The practical rule is to prefer neutral parents (scale of 1,1,1) for grouping unless intentional transformations are required.

keyIdea.title: Hierarchy rule
keyIdea.text: Children inherit transforms from parents. Use neutral parent transforms when grouping to avoid unintended distortion.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Parent & Child
Why use parenting
  • Coordinate movement: move one parent to move many children.
  • Organize scene hierarchy for clarity and performance.
  • Create grouped animations and assembly behaviors.
Example: An empty parent tracks a table; attach multiple props as children so they move together when the table adjusts in AR alignment.
Gotchas
Non-uniform parent scale will multiply into children and may distort meshes and colliders.
Reparenting changes local values; if you need to preserve world position, capture it before reparenting and restore local values after.
Key Takeaway

Use parent objects to group and control children, and avoid unintended distortion by keeping parent scale neutral when possible.

screens.title: Build a Simple Physics Scene
screens.subtitle: Step through creating a floor, cube, and bouncing sphere to see components in action.

narration.text: Let's walk through the hands-on physics demo from the chapter to solidify these concepts. Begin by creating a new scene and saving it, then add a Plane to act as the floor and set its position to zero. Next, create a Cube and place it at height Y=5 so it starts above the floor. The Cube will already include a Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer, and Box Collider. Select the Cube and use the Inspector to Add Component → Rigidbody so gravity will act on it. Press Play to observe the Cube fall and land on the Plane — this shows Colliders preventing overlap and Rigidbody enabling gravity. Stop the scene and experiment: change the Cube's Rigidbody Mass between 0.1 and 10 to feel how it alters impacts, then return to Play mode to compare. For the bouncing example, add a Sphere at a nearby position, attach a Rigidbody, then create a Physics Material named BouncyMaterial with Bounciness set to 1 and Bounce Combine to Maximum. Drag that Physics Material onto the Sphere's Collider Material slot. Play again and notice the Sphere bounces. A common gotcha is forgetting to assign the Physics Material to the collider slot — creating it in the Project is not sufficient. Save your scene when satisfied. This activity ties together Mesh, Collider, Rigidbody, and Inspector workflows into a simple, repeatable experiment.

keyIdea.title: Activity outcome
keyIdea.text: A simple scene demonstrates visibility, collision, and physics by combining Mesh, Collider, Rigidbody, and Physics Materials.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Physics Demo
Steps
  1. Create Plane → position (0,0,0) as ground.
  2. Create Cube → set position (0,5,0). Confirm Box Collider exists.
  3. Add Rigidbody to Cube. Play to observe gravity and collision.
  4. Create Sphere → add Rigidbody. Make Physics Material with high Bounciness and assign it to Sphere's Collider.
  5. Test different Mass and Collider settings and save the scene.
Troubleshoot
If objects pass through the floor, confirm both objects have Colliders and at least one has a Rigidbody. Also ensure Is Trigger is unchecked for solid collisions.
Try: change Rigidbody Mass on Cube to 10 and on Sphere to 0.1 to see the effect on collisions and feel of weight.
Key Takeaway

This simple scene demonstrates how Components combine to create visible, collidable, and physics-driven objects. Adjust settings to learn their effects.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Essentials to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts you should hold on to. First, GameObjects are empty containers; they define identity in the scene but not behavior. Second, Components are modular and attach to GameObjects to provide functionality: the Transform positions objects, Mesh Filter and Mesh Renderer create visible geometry, Colliders define boundaries for collisions, and Rigidbody enables physics responses. Third, the Inspector is your central workflow for adding, configuring, and removing Components; test changes in Play mode but remember Play-mode edits are not persistent. Fourth, parent-child hierarchies let children inherit transforms from parents — a powerful way to group and move related objects together. Keep these four ideas in mind as a checklist when building scenes: identity, composition, configuration, and hierarchy. A simple habit is to scan a problem object by checking: Does it have the required Mesh Filter and Renderer for visibility? Does it have a Collider for collision? Does it need a Rigidbody to respond physically? This checklist will catch most beginner issues quickly.

keyIdea.text: Identity → Composition → Configuration → Hierarchy: verify these to diagnose object behavior.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Key Concepts
GameObject
The empty container that identifies items in a scene. Components give it capability.
Components
Modular pieces like Transform, Mesh, Collider, Rigidbody, and scripts that you attach to GameObjects.
Transform
Mandatory on every GameObject; sets position, rotation, and scale. Local vs world coordinates matter.
Remember
When something behaves incorrectly, check these components: Mesh Filter & Renderer for visibility, Collider for collisions, Rigidbody for physics, and the parent chain for unexpected transforms.

narration.text: Finish with three compact reminders you can use while building. First, always check whether an object needs a Collider and a Rigidbody for physical interactions — visibility alone is not enough. Second, use the Inspector to add and tune Components, and remember Play-mode edits are temporary unless applied outside of Play. Third, organize using parent-child hierarchies and prefer neutral parent scales to avoid unintended distortion. These short rules are practical: they help you diagnose common errors quickly and make scenes easier to maintain. When in doubt, ask: does the object have the right Components to do the job? This simple checklist will speed up debugging and iteration in your AR/VR projects. Key Concepts — Quick Reference means collider + rigidbody for physics; inspector changes outside play are persistent; use neutral parents for grouping.. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Quick Reference
Collider + Rigidbody
Both are needed for physical interactions; collider defines shape, Rigidbody enables forces.
Inspector Edits
Make persistent edits outside Play mode. Use Play mode for testing only.
Hierarchy
Use neutral parents for grouping. Children inherit transforms and can simplify coordinated motion.
Final prompt
Before testing a scene, run a quick checklist: Mesh + Renderer for visibility, Collider for interactions, Rigidbody for physics, and parent settings for grouping.
